A specific, ownable idea: the world drawn as a clockwork map, with mechanical cities unfolding out of the terrain. Only this show could have it, and the idea carries the show's themes of power and machinery
Real material and light: engraved metal astrolabe bands, verdigris and brass, parchment map texture, hard sun flares through the armillary rings, and depth of field across miniature architecture
Choreography between frames: a camera flies over terrain, mechanisms rise and transform (the spiked tower, gear clusters), and it ends on a lit emblem with the title lockup
The credits are integrated into the world: each name sits in small spaced Trajan-style caps beside a house sigil and is placed in the scene's space rather than overlaid like a slide
A warm, deliberate palette (burnt gold, umber, desaturated green), held across every frame
gaps: Benchmark entry. The main title lockup is the most conventional frame: centred, symmetrical and flare-heavy
The credit typography is a classical serif with little scale contrast. It is correct but quiet compared with the world-building
The bloom and flare on the bookend frames is close to excessive and flattens the metal detail

tells: Reads as a real brand-system motion case study: it shows the motion techniques, dynamic layouts, animated glyph and physics principles of an established identity
The custom brand typeface and gradient are used on purpose, and there are systematic labels for each module (MOTION TECHNIQUES, PHYSICS)
The sticker and location-tag physics behaviour is a real system, not a placeholder

Weaknesses that drag it towards generic work: centred text on a gradient, a blurred colour blob behind the logo, a grid of placeholder-like cards and grey bars, and an end on the centred logo on white
gaps: It documents a system instead of telling a story. There is no single memorable idea or surprise comparable to A's world-as-mechanism
The frames are flat and shallow: gradients and blur stand in for light and material, with no texture or depth
The compositions are mostly centred, single-element frames, so little reads as a poster. It needs layered, dense frames where type, image and motion interlock

tells: A specific, memorable idea that belongs only to this piece: the world map rendered as a clockwork tabletop model that builds itself, held inside an astrolabe-like sphere, so the opening credits also work as a map of the story
Real material and light: engraved bronze bands with relief dragons, carved wood, brass gears, a warm sun-core glow that blows out the highlights and falls off into deep shadow

The type is integrated rather than placed: small-caps Trajan-like serif credits with sigil glyphs, set into the terrain at the right scale for each shot, then a bold flared logotype locked inside the metal band

Choreography across frames: an orbital band, then a low camera skimming the cities, a close-up of mechanisms, an overhead cartographic view, and a symmetrical logo resolve. Each frame changes scale and viewpoint and pushes the story forward
Limited palette of amber, bronze and muted slate-green that suits the subject; every frame works as a poster
gaps: Credit type is small and low-contrast against busy terrain in places (the map frame); a little more separation would help it read without hurting the integration
The logo lockup leans on a familiar bevelled, glowing epic-fantasy treatment that is less inventive than the mechanism sequence before it
The bloom on the sun-core frames clips heavily; a touch more highlight detail would keep the bronze texture in the brightest moments

tells: Reads as a brand motion-system case study (motion techniques, physics, dynamic layouts, animated glyph) with real system thinking behind it: physics diagrams, a type-on cursor and a sticker-style location tag
Uses the brand's own gradient and a custom, characterful grotesk, applied consistently across the system
But individual frames are close to the tells: a centred line of type on a gradient, a logo on a blurred colour blob, a lone logo on white, and grey placeholder bars in the physics panel
The structure is a presentation (labelled grid of panels), not a film; it explains the system rather than showing something you would remember
gaps: No single idea or moment of surprise; build one scene where the motion principles collide with real content instead of being shown as specimens in labelled boxes
Flat, effect-driven imagery (blur blob, gradient fill) with no light, material or depth; add tactile or photographic layers to match A's density
Composition repeats centred logo or line on a plain ground; push scale contrast and layered frames so each one stands as a poster

Mockup frames (TV in a lamp-lit room, UI grid) borrow their light from stock staging; design original images with controlled light and texture
Typography needs a point of view; a custom or more distinctive face and bolder interaction between bracket, type and footage would lift it beyond standard broadcast work

tells: A complete network rebrand toolkit: an 'ORIGINAL' bracket bug, a '9|8c' time lockup laid over live football footage, a programme end-card and a streaming UI shown on a TV in a room
The orange bracket device carries from the bug to the time divider to the end-card. That is a real, consistent system thought through by a broadcast design team
The live-action plates are graded and composited, and the UI is shown in a believable lived-in setting
It is let down by a generic grotesk headline ('Fboy Island') set like a slide, and by the empty white 'ORIGINAL' frame. This is solid package work, not a film
gaps: There is no central idea beyond 'apply the bracket'. It needs a visual metaphor tied to the network's attitude that runs through every frame, the way C's clockwork map does
The typography is a default-feeling grotesk. Commission or choose a display face so the time and title lockups have character, not just a logo colour
The frames are separate deliverables cut together. Choreograph transitions in which the bracket physically drives each cut, so it plays as one continuous piece

tells: A brand motion-principles film for Instagram, with labelled sections (motion techniques, physics, dynamic layouts, animated glyph) that show a documented motion system
The physics diagrams, typewriter caret and sticker pop ('TOKYO') suggest considered easing and interaction-level motion design
The proprietary brand gradient is used confidently, and the glyph resolve is clean

However, the gradient blob behind a centred logo and the centred headline on a gradient are exactly the generic tells. It is guideline documentation rather than an authored film, and it relies on the existing brand rather than a new idea
gaps: The ending of a logo on a gradient blob over white is the most predictable end-frame there is. It needs an image or concept that belongs to this film alone
The frames are flat UI planes with no material, light or depth. Build at least one moment with tactile texture or physical light
The grid of explanatory cards reads like a case-study deck. Turn the principles into one choreographed sequence instead of labelled demo tiles

tells: A singular idea: the world drawn as a clockwork map whose cities build themselves mechanically. It explains the story's geography and is unforgettable
Rich materials: engraved metal bands, wooden gears, a parchment map, and warm backlit sun flares with depth of field

The frames show clear choreography: the astrolabe band, the camera flying over the map, cities unfolding, and the resolve on the title emblem. Every frame works as a poster
gaps: The gold-and-sepia palette stays in a narrow range. A colder or contrasting accent region would add rhythm
Some credit placements are small and dissolve into busy textures, which hurts readability against detailed ground
The burst-of-light title card relies on a familiar epic-fantasy flare trope that is slightly less original than the rest

defects: The wordmark appears on a hard cut or pop between frame 1 and frame 2, with no visible build, anticipation or settle. The tagline is already on screen before it.
About 3 of the 4 seconds are a completely static hold. Per-second change is [16.9, 0, 0], so the film is mostly dead air.
In every pair, both frames are identical. There is no spacing, easing, overshoot, follow-through or motion blur anywhere.
The drop shadow is a flat, hard offset duplicate of the type in one solid colour. It has no softness, grain or misregistration, so it reads as a default effect and not as 70s print.
The background is flat vector cream with no paper texture, ink spread or halftone, even though the subject is a 70s print style.
A faint vertical seam or band in the background is visible at about x=185 on the left-hand frames. It may be a compositing edge or a gradient step.
The small tagline 'EST. 1974 · SLOW FOOD' is tiny, sits in the lower left with no relationship to the wordmark's grid, and does not move at all.
gaps: There is no choreography. A top studio would animate the wordmark itself: letters dropping in with squash and overshoot, the shadow sliding out after the face, a staggered wobble or swash suited to a 'groovy' 70s letterform. Here it is a single on/off cut followed by a 3 s freeze.

There is no arc and no idea. Nothing builds, peaks or resolves. The 'seventies' premise is never shown through motion (bounce, a rotoscope wobble, film gate weave, colour cycling), so the piece is a static logo card, not a film.

The finish has no material quality. Clean vector edges, a flat cream background and a hard-offset shadow have no print texture, grain, light falloff or registration error. For this period look the surface carries half the craft, and it is missing.
